articles.title: Lakers' Luka Doncic Reveals His Influence on Walker Kessler Trade, Talks With Rob Pelinka
articles.summary: While it had been reported throughout the offseason that Luka Dončić was a driving force in bringing Walker Kessler to the Los Angeles Lakers, the six-time All-Star has confirmed his discussions with general manager Rob Pelinka that prompted the sign-and-trade for the veteran center.
articles.body:
While it had been reported throughout the offseason that Luka Dončić was a driving force in bringing Walker Kessler to the Los Angeles Lakers, the six-time All-Star has confirmed his discussions with general manager Rob Pelinka that prompted the sign-and-trade for the veteran center.

Speaking to ESPN's Dave McMenamin , Dončić revealed he told the front office he wanted to play with Kessler:

"I told them after the season I wanted Walker. I think he's a really good player. Obviously, last season he didn't play. He played like five games. Obviously [Utah] kept him out, but just playing against him in the previous years, it was hard to score. He was protecting the rim, he was dominating the paint. So just after the season, I went to them and said, 'I want Walker.'"

How the Lakers Can Be 'Active' On Trade Market 🧠

The Lakers surprised many with how aggressive they went for Kessler. They sent two unprotected first-round draft picks and two pick swaps to the Utah Jazz in a sign-and-trade, then gave him a four-year, $130 million contract.

It was a huge price for a player who had not played more than 64 games in any of the previous three seasons and only became a full-time starter during the 2024-25 season.

Dončić knows as well as anyone how important a rim-running center can be because of how much of a difference Daniel Gafford made to the Dallas Mavericks when he was acquired midway through the 2023-24 campaign and helped spark their run to the NBA Finals that season.

Of the 130 two-man lineups that have played at least 320 minutes together so far this season, the Dončić-Kessler duo's plus-20.0 net rating ranks fifth. The four ahead of them are all San Antonio Spurs lineups, including three with Victor Wembanyama.

The addition of Kessler has helped the Lakers off to an NBA-best 15-3 start. It's their best record through 18 games since the 2019-20 season (16-2), which ended with them winning an NBA championship.

articles.title: LaMelo Ball Injured, Latest on T-Wolves Star's Status After Being Helped Off Court
articles.summary: Minnesota Timberwolves guard LaMelo Ball will miss Friday's game against the Memphis Grizzlies after suffering an ankle injury late in Wednesday's win against the Oklahoma City Thunder.
articles.body:
Minnesota Timberwolves guard LaMelo Ball will miss Friday's game against the Memphis Grizzlies after suffering an ankle injury late in Wednesday's win against the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Ball delivered a strong performance prior to the injury, recording 19 points on 7-of-18 shooting to go along with eight assists and seven rebounds.

Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic reported Wednesday night that Ball "was in very good spirits after the game, laughing and joking with teammates in the locker room" after the game.

Krawczynski added that Ball "seems to have avoided a major" injury.

Ball's injury is another blow to Minnesota. Superstar guard and face of the franchise Anthony Edwards has been out of the lineup and has been limited to only four games this season due to arthroscopic knee surgery.

With Edwards on the shelf, Ball has been the engine behind the Timberwolves' offensive attack, averaging 17.3 points per game to go along with 4.4 rebounds and a team-leading 5.7 assists and 1.6 steals.

During the offseason, Minnesota acquired Ball in a trade with the Charlotte Hornets, hoping he could be the ideal backcourt complement to Edwards.

It remains to be seen if that will be the case since Edwards has been out injured, but Ball has played a big role in keeping the T-Wolves afloat without Edwards, as they have still managed a 14-5 start, which is tied for third in the Western Conference.

With Ball out, much of the offensive burden would fall on the shoulders of Jaden McDaniels and Ayo Dosunmu, who are the Timberwolves' two leading scorers among players who have appeared in at least five games this season.

McDaniels was the star for Minnesota during Wednesday's win over OKC, leading all scorers with 32 points to go along with 10 rebounds and five assists.

Bones Hyland will likely see an uptick in playing time and importance in the event of Ball missing games as well.

articles.title: "¿Dónde están los equipos de la NBA Europa?"
articles.standfirst: Contundente diagnóstico del escéptico Ergin Ataman, seleccionador de Turquía y extécnico de Efes y Panathinaikos, al analizar el futuro del basket continental
articles.summary: Contundente diagnóstico del escéptico Ergin Ataman, seleccionador de Turquía y extécnico de Efes y Panathinaikos, al analizar el futuro del basket continental
articles.body: "Hablamos de la NBA Europa hace un año y seguimos en el mismo punto". Ergin Ataman no se muerde la lengua al analizar el futuro del baloncesto continental. En una entrevista concedida a La Gazzeta dello Sport, el seleccionador turco y exentrenador de Anadolu Efes y Olympiacos cuestiona los plazos y la falta de concreción del proyecto impulsado por la NBA: "¿Dónde están los equipos? ¿Dónde está Manchester? ¿Dónde está el equipo de Milán? ¿Dónde está el equipo de Londres? ¿Dónde está el PSG?". Su diagnóstico es contundente: "No es fácil crear equipos de primer nivel en dos o tres meses". El técnico de Estambul, de 60 años, respeta el poder económico de la NBA, pero pone en duda que sus responsables hayan entendido las particularidades del baloncesto europeo. "La NBA es la empresa deportiva más seria del mundo, pero cuando leo entrevistas con ejecutivos de la NBA Europa, me sorprende que no entiendan la mentalidad europea, la diferencia con la americana". Ataman admite que tiene "algunas dudas", aunque reconoce que "para nosotros, los profesionales, la llegada de una competición con todos estos recursos será una ventaja". Tampoco pasa por alto el nuevo escenario que prepara la Euroliga, con una ampliación a 24 equipos y la posibilidad de alcanzar los 28 en el futuro, organizados en conferencias. "Quizás también sea una estrategia contra la NBA Europa", apunta Ataman, que pone sobre la mesa el riesgo de una saturación de competiciones en el calendario continental. "Lo extraño sería una Euroliga de 24 equipos más los 16 de la NBA Europa, más la Eurocup, más la Champions League...". Una acumulación de torneos que le lleva a plantear una pregunta que afecta directamente al futuro de los protagonistas: «No sé dónde acabarán los jugadores». El reparto de talento y la carga de partidos aparecen así entre las grandes incógnitas de la nueva arquitectura del baloncesto europeo. Pese a sus reservas sobre el proyecto estadounidense, Ataman no reniega de la transformación de la Euroliga. "Me gusta la nueva Euroliga ampliada, soy optimista, pero será una situación nueva para todos". Un respaldo a la competición que convive con sus dudas sobre la NBA Europa y con una advertencia de fondo: el baloncesto continental se encamina hacia un cambio profundo, pero todavía tiene demasiadas preguntas sin respuesta.

articles.title: Heat's Bam Adebayo Gives Honest Quote on Giannis Partnership Amid 10-7 Start to 2026 NBA Season
articles.summary: When the Miami Heat paired Giannis Antetokounmpo with Bam Adebayo this offseason, the expectation was that it would propel them to instant contenders in the Eastern Conference.
articles.body:
When the Miami Heat paired Giannis Antetokounmpo with Bam Adebayo this offseason, the expectation was that it would propel them to instant contenders in the Eastern Conference.

After the Miami Heat suffered a 111-104 loss to the Philadelphia 76ers in Wednesday's NBA Cup matchup, Adebayo admitted the tandem is still trying to work on their on-court chemistry, according to South Florida Sun Sentinel's Ira Winderman .

"I think we still got a long way to go, but we're still figuring it out," Adebayo said. "We're still having pockets of moments where I feel like we're not as dominant as we should be, and we'll get better."

At their best, Adebayo believes the duo should be able to draw fouls and shut down opposing offenses.

"Obviously you get the ball, bucket, [draw a] foul," Adebayo said. "And when I get on the defensive end, obviously making sure that it's a hard time for you to score."

The Heat sent five draft picks and four players to the Milwaukee Bucks to acquire Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis in their blockbuster trade in July.

Miami lost its first four games of the 2026-27 season, but they have rebounded and won 10 of their last 13 games. Adebayo and Antetokounmpo showed their potential when they both scored 37 points in a 133-121 victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers. That performance made them just the second duo in franchise history to score 35-plus points in the same game, per the NBA .

Miami currently ranks sixth in the East heading into their Friday night matchup against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden.

articles.title: Knicks Announce Andre Drummond Decision Before Must-Win NBA Cup Game vs. Heat
articles.summary: Andre Drummond will miss Friday’s NBA Cup game against the Miami Heat after the Knicks center entered concussion protocol and was ruled out, according to a r...
articles.body:
Andre Drummond will miss Friday's NBA Cup game against the Miami Heat after the Knicks center entered concussion protocol and was ruled out, according to a report by James L. Edwards III of The Athletic .

His absence comes on a night when the defending Cup champions must win to stay alive in the Cup, and even a victory at Madison Square Garden may not be enough.

The NBA's 7:30 a.m. EST report still listed him as questionable (head). It also had OG Anunoby (calf) as doubtful, with Jordan Clarkson (foot) and Miles McBride (adductor) questionable, while Miami's Giannis Antetokounmpo (groin) was probable. Tipoff is 7 p.m. EST on Amazon Prime Video.

Knicks Lose Andre Drummond to Concussion

The injury occurred Wednesday against the Cleveland Cavaliers, when Drummond absorbed second-quarter contact to his head . He lasted until halftime but never came back, according to NBC Sports . James Wiseman took over his backup role, scoring six points.

Drummond logged three points and two rebounds in nine minutes. New York won 121-102.

Born Aug. 10, 1993, in Mount Vernon, New York, the 6-foot-11, 279-pounder played at UConn before the Detroit Pistons drafted him ninth overall in 2012 . He is a two-time All-Star and 2016 All-NBA Third Team pick who has won four rebounding titles. Over 985 career regular-season games, he has averaged 11.9 points and 11.8 rebounds. The Knicks are his seventh NBA team.

The NBA champions added him on a one-year contract worth a reported $3.8 million in July, after Mitchell Robinson left for the Boston Celtics. Backing up Karl-Anthony Towns, Drummond is averaging 3.7 points and 7.4 rebounds in 13.7 minutes over 18 games this season.

Knicks NBA Cup Scenarios Without Drummond

New York (12-6) sits third in the Eastern Conference , 2.5 games behind the Philadelphia 76ers, and has won six straight. Miami (10-7) is sixth.

In Cup play, New York fell 98-93 to the 76ers , then lost 106-104 to the Indiana Pacers before beating Cleveland. The Knicks are 1-2 in East Group B with a plus-12 point differential, and any loss Friday would eliminate them , according to Tom Dierberger of Sports Illustrated .

To take the group, New York needs to win by at least seven, get a Pacers victory over Philadelphia and prevail on tiebreakers. That would leave all five teams 2-2. A seven-point margin would also lift the Knicks to plus-19, one point ahead of Miami.

One wild-card route calls for a Knicks win, losses by the Pacers, Toronto Raptors, Detroit Pistons and Atlanta Hawks, and a tiebreaker edge over the second-place teams in East Groups A or C. But if the 76ers win and any of the Pistons, Raptors or Hawks also win, New York is out regardless of its own result.

Since the Cup began in 2023, no two-loss team has advanced to the knockout phase.

Coach Mike Brown also has an injury-thinned roster to manage.

"I'm trying to be smart about the minutes right now just overall," Brown said, as quoted by The Athletic .

Who's already into the knockout stage? Only the Dallas Mavericks (3-0), who have already locked up West Group A , according to Jon Metler of Covers .

Boston (3-0, plus-68) can win East Group C by beating Atlanta, and retains wild-card paths with a loss. Philadelphia (2-1) takes Group B by winning at Indiana. Miami (2-1, plus-25) can claim it by beating New York if the 76ers lose. The Heat could even take it while losing by six or fewer, provided Philadelphia falls and Miami owns the tiebreaker over Indiana.

As for wild cards, which go to each conference's best non-group winner, Detroit's plus-31 differential tops East contenders currently trailing group leaders , followed by Miami's plus-25.

articles.title: Spoelstra Risks Klay Thompson By Ignoring Tim Hardaway Jr.
articles.summary: Miami Heat coach Erik Spoelstra keeps Klay Thompson on the floor too long while Tim Hardaway Jr. sits. All U Can Heat says this unfair load hurts the team.
articles.body:
Coach Erik Spoelstra has placed an unfair burden on Klay Thompson by refusing to play Tim Hardaway Jr. in recent games. This stance ignores the fact that Hardaway Jr. is the only other reliable shooter on the roster. All U Can Heat reports that the Heat need to use Hardaway Jr. sooner to keep Thompson fresh for the long season ahead.

Thompson has been excellent since the first four games of the year. He shoots 43.6 percent from deep on 10 attempts per contest. He also averages 16.2 points in those games. Even with these strong numbers, the source argues that relying on one man is risky at his age. The team needs another quality shooter to take the pressure off Thompson immediately.

The problem came to a head during the loss to the Philadelphia 76ers on Wednesday. Thompson missed shots, and the offense stalled completely. The Heat needed another shooter to step up right then. Spoelstra tried to use Simone Fontecchio instead, but it did not work. Fontecchio missed wide-open looks in that game. Pelle Larsson also missed his chances. This failure highlights why the team needs Hardaway Jr. back in the rotation.

Hardaway Jr. has not played meaningful minutes in nearly two weeks. Spoelstra just is not comfortable turning to him yet. This makes it even harder for the coach to trust him in big moments later. The source notes that if the Heat want to be a real contender, Hardaway Jr. must evolve as a contributor. His return would help Spoelstra make better rotational choices and save Thompson's legs.

The 10-7 record hides a deeper issue. Yahoo Sports notes that the path to a title looks narrower than expected because the offense stops when Thompson misses. Relying on a single athlete to shoulder the burden versus top-tier foes is impossible for the squad. The defeat by the 76ers acted as a jarring reminder, echoing the season's difficult beginning.

Defense has also slipped against top wings. According to reports, reporters were informed that stars such as LeBron James require improved defense at the point of attack. The coach said, "Things become more real as the season goes on." He added that championship contenders never stop their process of improvement. Eastern Conference success without equilibrium may remain out of reach for the present roster composition.

Questions about player usage have arisen regarding Nikola Jovic. While he delivered a solid performance versus the Oklahoma City Thunder, he sat out the 76ers matchup. Such a scenario suggests Jovic lacks self-assurance when facing competition of the highest caliber. In the second half of that loss, Spoelstra utilized just eight players, excluding choices including Fontecchio and Jovic. The team faces the New York Knicks next.

articles.title: Game Preview: Gonzaga, Creighton Clash at the Players Era Festival
articles.summary: Nobody saw Creighton's Vegas run coming. Here's who they are, what they do well, and why the Zags should be ready.
articles.body:
The Zags opened the Players Era 16 by burying Kansas State 101-61, matching the event's record for margin of victory (the previous record doesn't matter and who cares about that anyway?). Two nights later they pulled away from Baylor 72-64, with Chauncey Wiggins hitting five threes off the bench and the defense holding the Bears without a basket for more than nine minutes of the second half.

That puts Mark Few's team in Friday night's bracket final at T-Mobile Arena (8 p.m. Pacific, ESPN), one win from Saturday's championship against either Tennessee or Louisville. The team standing in the way is Creighton, and these aren't the Bluejays Zag fans have come to know in recent years.

Creighton hasn't beaten Gonzaga since 1977. The Zags have won all four meetings since 2017, including a 90-63 win at the Kennel last season. The schedule adds a twist: the teams meet again December 12 in Omaha, so both staffs are preparing for this game with a rematch two weeks away.

Former Head Coach Greg McDermott retired after 16 seasons in Omaha, and the program handed the job to one of its own. Alan Huss played at Creighton in the late 1990s, spent six years as a McDermott assistant, then went 56-15 at High Point with two Big South titles and the Panthers' first NCAA Tournament bid. He's the first Creighton alum to coach the program since the early 1980s.

So far, so good. Creighton is 6-1, the best debut-season start for a Bluejay coach since the 1920s, and it already has neutral-floor wins over Iowa, Michigan and TCU. That's a long way from last season's 16-18 finish and a seventh-place pick in the Big East preseason poll.

Huss kept the "Let It Fly" offense McDermott built: pace, ball movement and lots of threes. Early this season, about half of Creighton's shots came from deep and they've shown no sign of changing the gameplan since arriving in Vegas.

The defense is where Huss has changed things. McDermott's teams sat back in drop coverage and tried not to foul. Huss wants disruption: more ball pressure, traps in chosen spots, and a "no middle" approach that pushes ball handlers toward the sideline. Creighton now ranks sixth nationally in defensive turnover rate, forcing a giveaway on roughly a quarter of opponent possessions.

Wes Enis, guard: The South Florida transfer started at Division II Lincoln Memorial and has been a high-volume shooter everywhere he's played. He leads Creighton at 18.1 points per game with a team-high 28 made threes on the season so far. Against Michigan he scored 30 points with eight threes, a Players Era record, and no turnovers. His percentages are modest (37.5 from the field, 36.4 from three), but he makes a lot of tough shots and wants the ball in his hands when the margins get tight. Against TCU he scored 17 of his 20 after halftime while fighting a flu that Huss said required three IV bags.

BJ Davis, guard. Possibly the Jays' best all-around player. The San Diego State transfer leads the team in steals and averages 15.4 points per game while shooting better than 48% from three on modest volume. He scored 15 against Gonzaga two years ago, back when he was in San Diego. He tweaked his calf on Thursday and played through it.

Austin Swartz and Hudson Greer: Swartz is a returning shooter who has turned into a capable passer, and he led the Jays with 18 points in the Iowa win. Greer, a sophomore, saves his best basketball for Las Vegas, where he's averaged 11.6 points. He had 13 points and four steals against TCU.

Katrelle Harmon, Point Guard: A four-star freshman who leads the team in assists and runs the second unit. He hit the winning free throw against Iowa.

Jackson McAndrew, Forward: A stretch four who was a preseason third-team All-Big East pick. He's playing on a sprained ankle, and foul trouble held him to six minutes against Michigan before he made three threes against TCU.

Oswin Erhunmwunse, Center: The Providence transfer, also a preseason third-team All-Big East selection, was brought in for rim protection. Watch his minutes: he played 13, 9, 11 and 11 in Creighton's four games against power-conference teams, and he picked up five fouls in 11 minutes against Michigan.

Jasen Green, Forward: A fifth-year senior from Omaha who calls himself a Swiss Army knife. He played the three, four and five against TCU and made the block and the free throws that saved the game.

After two home wins to open the season, Creighton lost 89-82 at Kansas State, the same team Gonzaga just beat by 40. K-State shot 57% and went 14-of-30 from three in that one. Five days later the 'Jays held on by a point against Iowa 70-69 in Des Moines, after the Hawkeyes erased a 12-point halftime deficit largely by getting to the free-throw line 33 times.

Then Creighton took apart the defending national champion. The Jays beat Michigan 99-73, hitting 16 threes (the most Michigan has ever allowed in a regular-season game) and scoring 27 points off 17 turnovers. A 22-2 run in the first half turned a six-point deficit into a rout.

Thanksgiving was a closer fight. Creighton led TCU by nine at halftime, then watched the Horned Frogs make their first seven threes of the second half. The game had 18 lead changes before Enis took over late and the Jays scored the final six points to win 95-87. Afterward Huss said TCU's Brock Harding had beaten his defense with ball screens in the middle of the floor. The Jays tried switching everything, a zone, double-teams on the ball and drop coverage, and "they really had an answer for all of it."

Take care of the ball. Everything Creighton does starts with turnovers. The Jays scored 27 points off them against Michigan and 20 against TCU, and they won transition scoring 22-9 on Thanksgiving. Gonzaga's 26 assists and eight turnovers against Kansas State is the standard, but Baylor's press rattled the Zags late Wednesday. Xaivian Lee, who had 11 points, 11 assists and nine rebounds in the opener, needs to keep his decisions quick and simple, move the ball before the traps arrive, and stay out of the sideline corners Creighton wants to push him into.

Go at the big men. Creighton fouls a lot. The Jays were called for 25 fouls against Michigan and 21 against TCU. When Erhunmwunse sits, Green or McAndrew moves to center, and TCU's bigger front line won the rebounding battle 37-31. Gonzaga has been outrebounding opponents by about 10 a game, and Braden Huff, Massamba Diop and Izan Almansa (5-of-5 against Baylor) can all score inside. Post up, crash the offensive glass, and get Creighton's bigs in foul trouble by halftime.

Own the defensive glass. A team that shoots this many threes gets a lot of long rebounds, and Creighton chases them. The Jays grabbed 13 offensive rebounds against Michigan, and against TCU Trevon Carter-Givens kept the game close with a putback in the middle of the second-half shootout. Gonzaga got away with a sloppy start against Baylor, which had eight offensive rebounds in the first half but turned them into just two points. Creighton won't be that wasteful. Every defensive possession has to end with a Gonzaga rebound: box out Green and Greer when they crash from the wing, have the guards come back to help, and limit Creighton to one shot per possession. Make the Jays score against a set defense every time, with no second chances, especially from outside.

Make Enis work, and live with some makes. He'll hit a few shots that look bad. The goal is to make him earn them: chase him off screens, contest every attempt, and don't foul him on threes (he got to the line nine times against TCU). Close out under control, too. Creighton loves driving past defenders who fly out at shooters, and that's where Davis does his damage. When the threes stop falling, the offense stalls; Creighton scored just 28 points in the second half against Iowa.

Win the bench minutes. Even with Javon Bennett out with a knee injury, Gonzaga's reserves outscored Baylor's 34-9, and Wiggins gives the Zags a 6-foot-11 shooter they didn't have two weeks ago. Creighton plays 10 deep but leans on veterans late, and Enis, Davis, McAndrew and Green are all playing through something. In a third game in four days, depth matters, especially against a team like Creighton who played three of their key starters for 34+ mins each the day before.

The advanced metrics see a wide gap here. Gonzaga is in the top six at EvanMiya and Bart Torvik, while Creighton sits in the 30s. Creighton has spent the week making that gap look smaller. The Jays are confident, banged up and opportunistic, and they've already beaten the defending champion by 26 and won a back-and-forth game with a very underrated TCU squad. If Gonzaga handles the pressure and makes the Jays defend the paint, it can control the game. If the Zags get careless with the ball or rattled by Creighton's defensive intensity, the Bluejays have shown it can turn a few turnovers into a big run quickly.

articles.title: Rapid Reaction: Northwestern’s comeback bid falls just short against DePaul in a 80-75 loss
articles.summary: DePaul managed to weather a fourteen point comeback from Northwestern, giving the ’Cats their fifth loss of the season.
articles.body:
Northwestern (4-5, Big Ten) women's basketball woke up early on Black Friday for a morning crosstown matchup against DePaul (8-1, Big East). The Wildcats, coming off two double-digits wins against Oakland and NIU, were seeking their first win over a power conference opponent, previously taking losses to Xavier and West Virginia.

They'd be denied by Zoey Ward and an offensive explosion by the Blue Demons. Ward led DePaul in with 19 points and 10 rebounds, marking her fifth double-double of the season. Kate Clarke scored 18, including the game-sealing free throws, and GIna Davorija dropped in 16 with three rebounds and two assists.

For Northwestern, Camdyn Nelson had her breakout game, scoring 20 points on just 11 shots from the field to group with eight assists, four rebounds and three steals. Lily Carmody got in foul trouble early, but rallied for 19 points in just 28 minutes on the floor.

After DePaul won the tip, Carmody quickly logged her first of two fouls in the first half. She and Jasmyn Cooper-Derba found themselves in limbo after early first-quarter mistakes. The Blue Demons seized early control with a second-chance three from Kate Clarke for the first basket of the game, then forced a Northwestern timeout with a full-court press.

Lexi Blue responded on the other end with a game-tying triple after the stoppage – the first of nine total threes that the two teams traded in the first quarter. Six unanswered from DePaul and another barrage of deep threes made the score 12-9 Blue Demons.

From there, both teams cooled off offensively. The 'Cats kept pace with the Blue Demons until the final minute of the first, when DePaul hit two consecutive threes to pull ahead, 29-19.

DePaul stretched its lead to as much as 14 in the second but later in the period, NU made four of five to reel the Blue Demons back to a 10 point deficit with 4:37 to play in the second.

After the media timeout, DePaul went on a three-minute scoring drought. Northwestern, and specifically Nelson, took the opportunity, facilitating fast-paced offense and providing strong perimeter defense en route to a 14-2 'Cats run over four minutes to pull within two of DePaul.

At the end of the first half, DePaul led 43-39. The Wildcats won the battle on the boards, led by a herculean effort by Kat Righeimer's seven, to propel themselves back into the game in the second quarter, while neither team found an offensive groove.

Nelson, who averages 7.8 points per game, scored 12 points with two rebounds, five assists and two steals. Carmody pitched a dozen points as well on 50% shooting from the field.

The difference between the two teams stayed within a handful of possessions through five and a half minutes of the third quarter, with the teams leaving few opposing buckets unanswered. Northwestern tied it up at 49 with 4:11 to go in the third quarter, marking the first time the game was tied since the start of the first quarter.

Northwestern took its first lead of the game just one minute later with Cooper-Derba's first three. She added another on the next offensive possession to push NU's lead to two. Nelson assisted both of the scores to get to eight on the day. However, DePaul found a four point swing to make it 57-55 heading into the fourth quarter.

With five minutes left in the fourth quarter, Nelson euro-stepped her way to the hoop to cut what was a five-point deficit to three. But DePaul responded with two of its own. Down the stretch, that was the story of the fourth: Northwestern fought for deuces, DePaul found a counter.

The teams exchanged two-pointers inside the three minute mark, but the 'Cats found true life with 1:10 on the clock, when Cooper-Derba scored a triple and DePaul was called for an off-ball foul right after. Nelson made both free throws, and with a minute left, the score was 74-73. DePaul called a timeout, feeling the victory being pulled from its grasp.

After the timeout, Clarke and Nelson traded jumpers late in their teams' respective possessions. But with 16.1 seconds remaining, Northwestern was forced to foul. Unfortunately for the 'Cats, they'd send Gina Davorija to the line, an 84% shooter from the line. She made both, handing Northwestern the ball, a three point deficit and fifteen seconds to work with.

Northwestern's last chance to tie ended with Harter's shot from the corner, which found nothing but iron. Mikaia Litza snagged the competitive rebound, effectively sealing the game with 2.4 seconds to go. Northwestern fouled, and Clarke completed the win by making both of her free throws to finalize a 80-75 win for the Blue Demons.

Northwestern has one more opportunity to get back to .500 before the start of Big Ten play, when they face Illinois State on November 30th at 6 p.m. CT. The game will be aired on Big Ten Plus.

articles.title: Mizzou women’s basketball falls to Tulane after second-half collapse
articles.summary: struggles against quality opponents hurts Mizzou women’s basketball against Tulane
articles.body:
Missouri women's basketball had another opportunity to prove it could compete against a quality opponent. Instead, the Tigers watched another promising start turn into a disappointing loss.

Mizzou fell 80-64 to Tulane on Friday at the Ocean Center in Daytona Beach, Florida, suffering its second loss against a competitive opponent this season. The defeat followed a similar pattern to its loss against Kansas State, with the Tigers struggling to maintain their momentum once the game became more demanding.

The Tigers entered halftime tied 35-35 with Tulane after an evenly matched first half. Mizzou showed flashes of an offense capable of keeping pace, but the second half exposed problems that ultimately put the game out of reach.

Tulane outscored Mizzou 45-29 after halftime, including a 25-15 advantage in the fourth quarter. The Green Wave steadily took control while the Tigers struggled to find consistent offense or slow down their opponent defensively.

The biggest difference came from beyond the arc. Tulane shot 10-of-17 from 3-point range, good for 58.8%, while Mizzou made just 3 of its 16 attempts. The Green Wave particularly caught fire in the second half, connecting on seven of its nine 3-point attempts.

Mizzou also struggled to generate enough offense when its outside shots were not falling. The Tigers finished 21-of-62 from the field, shooting 33.9%, compared to Tulane's 49.2% mark. Turnovers contributed to the problem, with Missouri committing 18 compared to Tulane's 15.

The Green Wave capitalized on those mistakes, scoring 21 points off turnovers. Tulane also received a significant boost from its bench, outscoring Mizzou's reserves 30-6.

Grace Slaughter led Missouri with 19 points, while Khloe Ford added a career high 21 points and 12 rebounds. Nevaeh Caffey contributed 11 points, but the Tigers could not find enough production across the roster to match Tulane's offensive balance.

The loss raises questions about Mizzou's ability to sustain its play against stronger competition. The Kansas State game provided an earlier warning, and Friday's second-half collapse offered another example of the Tigers struggling to respond when an opponent gains control.

Mizzou can point to a competitive first half, but that will offer little consolation after being outscored by 16 points over the final 20 minutes. Against teams capable of consistently making shots and punishing mistakes, the Tigers have yet to show they can maintain their level of play for an entire game.

articles.title: Six takeaways from UVA basketball’s 83-71 win over Xavier
articles.summary: Analyzing Virginia’s win over the Musketeers, which gave the ’Hoos their first 9-0 start since the 2018-19 title team.
articles.body:
Less than two days after outlasting Marquette in a game interrupted by a leaking roof, No. 2 Virginia was back on the floor at Imperial Arena on Friday morning. Its opponent had an even shorter turnaround. Wednesday's rain delay pushed Xavier's opener against Texas A&M back nearly two hours, and the Musketeers held off the Aggies 88-83 that evening behind 20 points and 10 rebounds from Mike Nwoko. Under second-year coach Richard Pitino, Xavier came in 6-1, with its only loss coming at Iowa, and with a defense that was forcing 16 turnovers and 13.1 steals per game. DraftKings opened Virginia as an 8.5-point favorite, but the line had fallen to 6.5 by tipoff.

The roof held up this time, and so did Virginia. The Cavaliers never trailed, built a 42-27 halftime lead and led by as many as 19. Xavier won the second half 44-41 and got within nine late, but Elijah Gertrude answered with back-to-back threes, and Virginia closed out an 83-71 win in front of 1,139 fans. Sam Lewis led the way with 21 points, eight rebounds, four assists, two steals and two blocks.

Virginia moved to 9-0 and covered both the opening and closing spreads. Xavier fell to 6-2.

Virginia is off to its best start since the national championship season

The last time Virginia started 9-0 was 2018-19, when Tony Bennett's team won its first 16 games on the way to the national title. Since then, the closest any Virginia team came was 2022-23, which started 8-0 before losing to Houston on Dec. 17. The 2019-20 team started 7-0 before losing at Purdue.

What stands out about this start is how many ways Virginia has found to win. It beat an athletic Arkansas team by 19 in Washington, came back from 11 down at halftime in front of a raucous crowd at Maryland behind a career day from Lewis, survived an hour-and-35-minute rain delay against Marquette and, on Friday, won comfortably despite turning it over 21 times. Ryan Odom is now 39-6 at Virginia.

On a day when Xavier did everything it could to speed Virginia up, Lewis stepped up to lead the 'Hoos. He hit a three off a pick from Johann Grünloh on an inbounds play in the first half, blocked a three to force a shot-clock violation, turned a steal into a breakaway dunk and, with a possession going nowhere midway through the second half, bailed Virginia out with a rhythm-dribble step-back three. He finished 7-of-15 from the field and committed only two turnovers on a day when his teammates struggled to hold onto the ball.

The last two games have not been pretty, and I will get to why below. But a team that can play this sloppy for stretches and still win by 12 against a Big East opponent that had just knocked off Texas A&M, a team that started the season in KenPom's top 20, is a team with a high floor. That is a good sign this early in the season, and a good indication that this team can play well on consecutive days in a tournament.

Elijah Gertrude set a career high for the second time this month

Gertrude scored 17 points on 6-of-11 shooting and 4-of-9 from three in 23 minutes. His previous career high was 14, which he set against Old Dominion on Nov. 17. His four made threes are also a career high, one more than he made against Northeastern and Old Dominion. Gertrude's ability to knock down the three continues to be one of the biggest revelations of this season. I feel the need to remind fans that this is a player who came into the season 3-of-29 from three for his career.

He also did it in every way he could. In the first half, he hit a three off a De Ridder drive-and-kick, used a pump fake and a side step to create another and finished a reverse layup off a great find from Chance Mallory on a cut. His biggest moment came late. After a Tru Washington three cut the lead to nine, Gertrude hit a three off good ball movement, then took a swing pass from Mallory in the corner and buried another for the career high. This was essentially the double dagger that put the game to bed, with Virginia up 15 and around four minutes to go.

It was not perfect. He picked up three fouls, including a foul on an inbounds pass and a reach-in when he came flying over to try for a steal. But after three years of knee rehab and garbage time, Gertrude has become the first player off the bench and one of the most dependable shooters on the roster.

Jan Vide had his best game as a Cavalier

Vide scored a season-high 12 points without missing a shot, going 4-of-4 from the field and 4-of-4 at the line in 18 minutes. He added two rebounds, an assist, a steal and a block.

What I liked most was how he scored. It was well known coming in that Vide was not a good three-point shooter. He went just 8-of-29 from three at Loyola Marymount last season, where he averaged 12.1 points and 4.0 assists. Many wondered how he would fit in an Odom offense that prioritizes spacing and the three ball. However, despite taking only one three all season, he showed Friday how valuable he can be.

Instead, he lived in the mid-range. He finished a fallaway push shot on the right side after a broken play, hit a floater off a good find, drove the length of the floor for a pull-up jumper and drew a foul, and bailed Virginia out with about two seconds left on the shot clock with another mid-range pull-up. He also made a smart entry pass to Lewis, followed it and grabbed the rebound among the big men for a putback. Late in the game, he drew Nwoko's fourth foul and made both ends of the one-and-one. He may not have much range, but he has an incredibly smooth shot and excellent touch on floaters and push shots as he drives.

The other thing is his ball handling and size. He is a steady presence with the ball, a contrast to Mallory's 100-percent-all-the-time mentality. Moreover, at 6-foot-6, he can see over defenders, and he has shown on multiple occasions an excellent ability to find the open man, even on cross-court passes that lead to open shots. Ball handling off the bench had been an area to watch for me, and it seems clear after the last two games that Vide is the answer.

His previous season high in points was eight, against Loyola Maryland, and his 18 minutes were also a season high. This was the second straight game Vide has played real minutes as Mallory's backup, which is notable given the increased level of competition. Against Marquette, he did not score but had three steals and again helped Virginia handle the press. Before the Bahamas, his minutes had come and gone: 17 against Bucknell, then three at Maryland and two against Old Dominion.

The turnovers keep coming in bunches, and the fouls did not help

Virginia turned it over 21 times, a new season high, three more than the 18 it committed against Marquette. That is 39 turnovers in two games in the Bahamas, after 11 combined against Old Dominion and Loyola Maryland.

The start was ugly. Virginia turned it over on five straight possessions and, four minutes into the game, had taken only two shots. Nolan Adekunle was called for an illegal screen, Mallory was trapped and had to throw the ball off a defender out of bounds, entry passes were picked off and Kalu Anya traveled on a double-clutched pass. By my count, that was seven turnovers in the first 10 or so minutes. Then Virginia settled down and went the final nine and a half minutes of the half without one, which is how it built a 15-point lead.

The second half was sloppy again. De Ridder lost the ball on a spin move, and Xavier took it the other way for a layup to finish a 7-0 run. Washington poked the ball away from Lewis on a drive. Mallory lost his handle, and Xavier stole an inbounds pass when he tried to dribble through traffic. Xavier finished with 15 steals, two more than its season average, and won the points-off-turnovers battle 15-7. Virginia had just four steals of its own, its fewest this season. This continues a recent trend of Virginia struggling mightily against physical, intense ball pressure.

The fouls added to it. The final count was close, 21 on Virginia to 20 on Xavier, but Xavier lived at the line, going 18-of-29 to Virginia's 17-of-22, and was in the double bonus for the final 8:20. Some of the calls were tough, including a foul away from the ball on Anya while he was the one on the floor holding his face.

To be fair, one problem from Wednesday was fixed. After Marquette grabbed 21 offensive rebounds, Xavier had just nine on 37 missed shots, even though offensive rebounding had been a strength for the Musketeers in their previous game. Virginia won the rebounding battle 46-26 despite not having Grünloh for much of the second half. Shooting 51 percent from the field and 12-of-30 from three covered for a lot. However, Virginia will need to clean up the turnovers and fouls going forward.

Two days after playing a career-high 39 minutes, Grünloh had two points on 1-of-3 shooting, three rebounds and a block in 20 minutes. He was solid early, securing a couple of defensive rebounds and blocking Washington at the rim, but the fouls piled up. A pump fake got him in the air in the first half, and early in the second half, he was caught out of position on a rebound and picked up his fourth, which sent him to the bench. He checked back in when Nwoko picked up his own fourth with under seven minutes left.

Adekunle's foul trouble came even earlier. He picked up two fouls in the first four minutes, the second on an illegal screen, and played just 10 minutes, with three points, three turnovers and three fouls.

De Ridder finished with a double-double, 14 points and 10 rebounds, and he hit two of the best shots of the game, a deep three to break a scoring drought in the first half and a pump-fake, side-step three to open the second. But he went 5-of-12, committed four turnovers and lost the ball several times trying to attack in the post.

Xavier took advantage. Nwoko scored 15 points in 20 minutes, made 7-of-10 free throws and at one point scored nine straight for the Musketeers. Xavier won the paint 30-26. With Favour Ibe still away from the team because of his visa situation, Anya played 20 minutes, up from three on Wednesday, and finished with four points and five rebounds. Virginia's frontcourt depth has been tested in the Bahamas, and it will be good to have Ibe back in case of more foul trouble going forward.

Chance Mallory continues to hustle like crazy

Mallory finished one assist and two rebounds shy of a triple-double, with 10 points, eight rebounds and a season-high nine assists in 34 minutes, and the broadcast named him its player of the game. His previous best this season was six assists, which he had four times.

The rebounding is the part that keeps surprising me. Before this week, his career high was eight. He grabbed 12 against Marquette and eight more Friday, which gives him 20 in two games. He scooted in for an offensive rebound late in the second half to keep a possession alive, and he made a great save on a broken play in the first half that led to a Vide basket.

He also kept making plays for others. He found Gertrude on a cut for a reverse layup, swung the ball for Gertrude's career-high three and set up De Ridder for a layup. When Virginia needed a basket, he called his own number on a pull-up three to push the lead to nine in the first half, and he knocked down a corner three off a no-look pass from Anya in the second. He went 4-of-4 at the line, and he even blocked a three from behind after a missed steal attempt.

The one blemish was the five turnovers, a team high. But Mallory has a nose for the ball, and Virginia needs his energy as much as his scoring.

Virginia was not the only ACC team to pick up quality wins this week. No. 25 Louisville beat No. 5 Texas Tech 72-64 on Tuesday at the Players Era Festival, then beat St. John's 93-90 on Thursday on an Adrian Wooley walk-off three. No. 16 Duke beat No. 10 UConn 77-63 on Wednesday in Las Vegas, which is worth noting since Virginia plays UConn at Madison Square Garden on Dec. 20. Pitt moved to 8-0 with a 71-64 win over DePaul at the Fort Myers Tip-Off, No. 17 Miami beat Michigan 97-70 and Boston College moved to 7-0 on a game-winner against UCF.

After a season in which Virginia went 1-4 against ranked opponents, a stronger ACC means more chances for quality wins come conference play. Virginia plays Duke twice, hosts Louisville and visits Miami.

Bonus: Virginia passed two physical Big East tests

Last November, Virginia lost to Butler in a resort ballroom at The Greenbrier. This week, it went 2-0 against Big East teams in another one. Marquette and Xavier both pressured the ball, crowded the passing lanes and made Virginia uncomfortable for long stretches. Virginia turned it over 39 times and allowed 26 steals in the two games and still won both. Odom will not like the turnovers, but this team knows how to win games that do not go its way.

Virginia gets five days off before hosting Kentucky on Wednesday, Dec. 2, at 7:15 p.m. ET on ESPN in the SEC/ACC Challenge. After that, it hosts Bethune-Cookman on Dec. 8 and Western Carolina on Dec. 13 before facing No. 10 UConn at Madison Square Garden on Dec. 20. ACC play opens at Clemson on Dec. 29.

The turnovers have to come down, and Virginia needs Grünloh and Adekunle to stay out of foul trouble. But for the first time since the 2018-19 team, Virginia is 9-0, and it has gotten there against a schedule that has tested it in just about every way possible.

articles.title: No. 7 Texas to face Saint Mary’s in the Rady Children’s Invitational championship
articles.summary: The Gaels hit 15 threes to upset the Bruins on Thursday.
articles.body:
Thursday's 92-83 win over the Georgetown Hoyas sent the No. 7 Texas Longhorns through to the championship game of the Rady Children's Invitational championship on Friday against the Saint Mary's Gaels.

Recovered from a glute strain that limited him to four minutes in Sunday's win over Southern Indiana, Texas sophomore guard Isaiah Johnson scored a game-high 26 points to led the Horns over the Hoyas, including seven second-half free throws. Johnson also tied his career high with four steals and dished out four assists.

Johnson's 26 points matched his season high set against Baylor — in the two biggest games Texas has played so far, Johnson has often looked like the best player on the court, setting a standard of stepping up in important moments as the Longhorns begin creating their NCAA Tournament resume.

The performance was all the more crucial because the team's other star, junior center Matas Vokitetaitis, had one of his worst games at Texas, fouling out in 13 minutes after scoring only five points. After spending the offseason focused on avoiding foul trouble to be able to play more minutes, Vokietaitis operated without the discipline that head coach Sean Miller expects from him.

"Matas, he didn't do anything today. He had the day off, Miller said . "Matas wasn't able to play for us today."

With Vokietaitis limited to four minutes in the second half, freshman forward Marcus Spears Jr. played at a high level — in 16 second-half minutes, Spears scored 12 of his career-high 18 points on 5-of-7 shooting.

"It took us some time, but I'm very proud of our team's resilience," Miller said. "We were far from perfect, but I thought Isaiah Johnson was terrific, and I really thought that Marcus Spears and David Punch, those two guys together without Matas, did just a really, really good job."

Punch recorded his first double-double for the Longhorns with 11 points and 10 rebounds while also notching five assists, two blocks, and two steals.

After taking control of the game with a 15-3 run at the end of the first half, Texas was able to hang on despite committing 16 fouls over the final 20 minutes that led to 21 made free throws by Georgetown in the second half.

Saint Mary's will challenge Texas to play better defense without fouling on Friday after notching an 85-70 upset of No. 6 UCLA in the second game of the invitational, keyed by 15 made threes, another area in which the Gaels will challenge the Longhorns.

The guard-centric attack was led by 21 points by Jeremy Dent-Smith, who hit a team-high five threes against UCLA. Backcourt mates Mantas Juzenas and Joshua Dent both added 18 points, with Dent turning in an efficient performance, making all three of his three-point attempts and hitting 7-of-9 shots overall.

The three-point barrage started early — six of the first seven buckets made by the Gaels were triples as they hit 10 total in the first half.

So Texas will have to be sharp with its rotations and closeouts early in the game because Saint Mary's averages more than 27 three-point attempts per game, 10 more than Miller's team, which leans much more heavily on scoring in the paint.

The massive three-point volume reflects the philosophy of first-year head coach Mickey McConnell, a Saint Mary's alum who played for and then served as an assistant under longtime head coach Randy Bennett, who left Moraga for Tempe to take over the Arizona State program in March.

The Gaels don't just take a lot of threes, they make a lot of them, too, ranking seventh nationally in three-point shooting percentage at 44.1 percent, aided by crisp ball movement that generates assists on almost two thirds of their made baskets, 17th in the country.

Dent and guard Darius Bivins both have assist rates of 25 percent.

The combination of a quicker pace and distance shooting acumen allows Saint Mary's to average 93.8 points per game, up almost 14 points from last season.

Since suffering an overtime loss to Nevada in Lake Tahoe, McConnell's team has ripped off five straight wins, establishing the Gaels as a dangerous team capable of pulling off another upset in San Diego.

According to BartTorvik.com, the win probability for Texas on Friday is 60 percent.

articles.title: LaMelo Ball injury news: Timberwolves announce update for Grizzlies game
articles.summary: The Minnesota Timberwolves have provided a final update on LaMelo Ball's status for tonight's game against the Memphis Grizzlies.
articles.body:
LaMelo Ball 's availability for the Minnesota Timberwolves ' matchup against the Memphis Grizzlies was uncertain after he suffered an ankle injury in Wednesday's win over the Oklahoma City Thunder .

The Timberwolves were waiting to see how the guard responded before making a decision on his status. His absence would be another setback for Minnesota, which is already without Anthony Edwards .

Minnesota has now made its decision, ruling Ball out of Friday night's game against Memphis with a left ankle sprain.

LaMelo Ball ruled out against the Grizzlies

The Timberwolves announced that Ball will not play against the Grizzlies.

Ball went down with 2:29 remaining in the fourth quarter after landing on Isaiah Hartenstein's foot while battling for a rebound. He needed assistance to leave the court and did not return.

Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch admitted after the game that the injury did not look good, although he did not have an immediate assessment of its severity.

Ball finished the contest with 19 points, seven rebounds and eight assists before leaving with the injury. His absence leaves Minnesota without another important piece of its backcourt.

Timberwolves face another challenge without LaMelo Ball

Minnesota will have to adjust its backcourt rotation against Memphis, with Anthony Edwards already sidelined following right knee surgery.

Ayo Dosunmu and Bones Hyland could take on larger roles in the backcourt against the Grizzlies.

The Timberwolves enter Friday's matchup with a 3-0 record in West Group B play. A victory over Memphis would secure their place in the next round.

articles.title: New NBA Trade Rumors on Kristaps Porzingis as Insider Updates State of Warriors' Talks
articles.summary: Golden States Warriors center Kristaps Porzingis stepped away from basketball to prioritize his health, but teams may still have incentive to acquire him in a trade.
articles.body:
Golden States Warriors center Kristaps Porzingis stepped away from basketball to prioritize his health, but teams may still have incentive to acquire him in a trade.

During Friday's episode of the ALL NBA podcast (27:49 mark of video), Marc Stein and Adam Mares discussed potential opportunities for the Warriors to trade Porzingis ahead of February's trade deadline.

According to Stein, Porzingis' contract "holds appeal to teams that are facing financial troubles." The 31-year-old has a two-year, $40 million contract that includes $20 million this season and only $3 million guaranteed in 2027, per Spotrac .

Stein reported that Porzingis is open to a buyout, and a team that trades for his contract and buys him out could save themselves "millions and millions of dollars."

"Even saying all of that, it's easier said than done for a trade to materialize," Stein said.

Teams in discussion with the Warriors about a potential trade for Porzingis "want Golden State to sweeten trade offers with draft picks," according to Stein.

"The Warriors have to decide, 'Do we want to put draft compensation into an in-season deal?' or 'Do we want to keep all our draft compensation for maybe off-season swings that might be more grandiose?'" Stein said.

Golden State might have some incentive to find a trade partner sooner rather than later. A player traded before December 16 can be used to match salaries in a future trade before February's trade deadline, according to Luca Evans of the San Francisco Chronicle .

First of all, yes, it does seem like we are going to normalize Ryan Conwell going off.

Second of all, three-point shooting was the biggest difference in that first quarter. New York is 2-of-11 from beyond the arc while Miami is a scorching-hot 6-of-11.

Score: Heat 31, Knicks 21 | End of the first quarter

Is this that stat-padding thing Victor Wembanyama was talking about?

Score: Heat 28, Knicks 19 | 57.0 seconds remaining in the first quarter

Ryan Conwell was drafted 37th overall and has already proven to be a credible rotation player for Miami. Typical Heat.

Score: Heat 25, Knicks 16 | 2:02 remaining in the first quarter

Now the Knicks are Forcing the Heat to Group

Miami has called a timeout after a quick 4-0 by the Knicks. This mini burst has coincided with New York inserting Pacome Dadiet and having him guard Giannis.

Score: Heat 15, Knicks 11 | 5:22 remaining in the first quarter

KAT was questionable before the game with an abdominal injury, so this is something to keep an eye on.

With Andre Drummond recovering from a concussion, James Wiseman is the Knicks' only other true big. And with Anunoby also out due to a calf strain, New York doesn't even have OG-at-the-5 units in its back pocket.

Score: Heat 15, Knicks 9 | 6:28 remaining in the first quarter

This three to open the game from Klay was just the beginning. He and Bam have combined to score 13 of the Heat's first 15 points. After a Giannis Antetokounmpo finish at the rim, the Knicks have called their first timeout.

Score: Heat 15, Knicks 7 | 7:03 remaining in the first quarter

We are underway, and the Heat's offense looks good .

Klay Thompson already has two threes, and Bam Adebayo dropped in his first triple. Miami's speed has the Knicks scrambling. The offense overall is averaging 1.63 points per possession in the early going.

Score: Heat 13, Knicks 7 | 7:41 remaining in the first quarter

High Praise for Klay Thompson from a Heat Legend

This feels over the top, but I get what he's saying. Miami's offense is thermonuclear with Klay firing away so often from deep.

The Knicks' Path to the NBA Cup Knockout Round

Of all the different scenarios in play, the Knicks beating the Heat by at least seven points and then seeing Indy upset Philadelphia is their cleanest path to the next round.

Here's How The Heat Can Clinch an Appearance in the Knockout Round

Basically, Heat fans should definitely be rooting for Miami and Indiana to win. Milwaukee downing Detroit would be just a bonus.

With Giannis Antetokounmpo cleared to play, the Heat are rolling out what's become their go-to starting unit. This group is now their second-most used lineup on the season and outscoring opponents by a whopping 20.8 points per 100 possessions .

Karl-Anthony Towns playing basketball is always a good thing for the Knicks. But it's a particularly good thing when they're already down OG Anunoby and Deuce McBride, not to mention Andre Drummond.

articles.title: Former NBA lottery pick Rob Dillingham gets punched by Wizards rookie Felix Okpara during G League game
articles.summary: Okpara threw a punch at Dillingham after being shoved with no call from the officials. A melee then broke out among players from both G League teams.
articles.body:
Playing for the G League Westchester Knicks, former NBA first-round pick Rob Dillingham was involved in a scuffle during Friday's matchup with the Capital City Go-Go.

In the fourth quarter of Westchester's 125-104 win , Dillingham was punched by Capital City center Felix Okpara at the top of the 3-point line. Dillingham pushed Okpara on his way down the court, and the center looked at the official for a foul call.

When one wasn't made, Okpara clotheslined Dillingham across the neck and shoulders, knocking him to the floor.

Both teams then gathered in a scrum past the Westchester basket, going off the court as Okpara backpedaled toward the baseline. Coaches, officials and arena security personnel then separated each group of players.

Ermal Kuqo, the Knicks' senior director of minor league operations, and his 6-foot-10, 270-pound frame also got involved, which surely helped provide a significant obstacle to fisticuffs.

Dillingham and Okpara were subsequently both ejected from the game. Dillingham finished with 10 points and 8 assists, while Okpara scored 12 points with 9 rebounds for the Go-Go.

Okpara was the Washington Wizards' second-round pick in the 2026 NBA Draf t , selected No. 46 overall out of Tennessee. In three games with the Wizards, he averaged one point and 0.7 rebounds in five minutes of play. In the G League, Okpara is scoring 11.4 points, 8.8 rebounds and 2.4 blocks per game.

Dillingham was the San Antonio Spurs' 2024 first-round pick, selected No. 8 overall out of Kentucky. He was traded to the Minnesota Timberwolves on draft night for a first-round pick swap in 2030 and first-rounder in 2031.

Last season, the T-Wolves dealt him midway through his second season in a trade involving Ayo Dosunmu going to the Chicago Bulls . Before training camp this season, he was moved to the Charlotte Hornets in exchange for Buddy Hield but was subsequently waived. In November, he signed with the New York Knicks' G League team .

In three games with Westchester, Dillingham is averaging 21 points and 6.3 assists per game while shooting 35% on 17 3-point attempts.

articles.title: Stephen Curry Injury Update, Latest on Warriors Star's Return Timeline as Star Makes 'Good Progress'
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry is making "good progress" as he continues to rehab an oblique abdominal tear, and he will be re-evaluated again on Wednesday, the team announced on Friday.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry is making "good progress" as he continues to rehab an oblique abdominal tear, and he will be re-evaluated again on Wednesday, the team announced on Friday.

Curry is now set to miss at least the next three games.

The two-time NBA MVP exited the Golden State's 115-108 loss to the Houston Rockets on Nov. 11 with right abdominal soreness. Coach Steve Kerr said immediately after the game that the "concern is high," though the extent of the injury wasn't yet known.

The Warriors are off to a 10-8 start so far, and Curry is a big reason for that. He's averaging 27.8 points and shooting 45.7 percent from beyond the arc.

Needless to say, losing the veteran point guard for a stretch of games would be a serious blow.

Golden State is still waiting for Jimmy Butler to return from a torn ACL. Kristaps Porziņģis has yet to make his season debut after taking an indefinite leave from basketball. Rookie forward Yaxel Lendeborg has been better than expected out of the gate, but the Warriors' hopes of contending continue to rest squarely on Curry's shoulders.

Missing the 12-time All-Star for only a few games may not seem like much, but the margins in the competitive Western Conference could be slim by the end of the year. Four games were the gap between the sixth-place Minnesota Timberwolves and the Phoenix Suns, who fell into the play-in tournament.

For the Warriors, there's simply no replacing Curry, and that has been the case for over a decade. Even at their peak, Kerr struggled to build an effective Curry-less lineup.

That hasn't changed with Golden State's championship window slowly closing over the last few seasons.

articles.title: Knicks’ Mike Brown toasts Tyler Nickel for ‘physical’ surprise debut vs. Cavs
articles.summary: NEW YORK — 2026 Emirates NBA Cup Group Play continued on Wednesday night. New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown treated his team’s game against the Cleveland...
articles.body:
NEW YORK — 2026 Emirates NBA Cup Group Play continued on Wednesday night. New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown treated his team's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers like a science experiment. In other words, it was business as usual for New York despite the higher stakes.

These Knicks simply aren't as desperate or hungry as they were at this time last year. Their 2025 NBA Emirates Cup victory proved in a small sample size that they were capable of winning at a high level. The ultimate vindication for their players and staff, however, came along with the 2026 NBA Finals Trophy they earned in June. New York is more focused on defending that title than the one they won in Las Vegas.

Without organizational pressure to maximize their point differential this time around, Brown turned to the least experienced player on his bench to help give his Knicks an edge. Rookie sharpshooter Tyler Nickel, in his first opportunity at the NBA level, scored five points on 2-3 FG in nine minutes. His coach told reporters at Madison Square Garden that the 23-year-old wasn't on his minutes sheet going into the game, but delivered exactly what he was looking for when called upon.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"I just thought we needed a lift from some place. I thought if he came in and hit a three, the bench would get into it. It would kind of get everybody hyped. And it could help us with a little bit of a momentum shift, if that could happen. And he did. He did more than that…he was a physical presence. He was just running around and running into people, going at 100 mph, and it was beautiful to see. We needed to shift the momentum in the physicality area. And he brought a lot of that to the table in his 8.5 minutes," Brown said postgame.

Knicks earned these stress-tests of their depth with NBA title win

Nickel was certainly not perfect in his first NBA minutes. The rookie was thrown into an important stretch, of an important game, against the same opponent his team bested in last season's Eastern Conference Finals. He made one of his two attempts from behind the 3-point line, which was good; he also committed four personal fouls, which was not.

Brown didn't mind at all. The coach added after the game that Nickel's errors were made with — or as the result of playing with — gusto.

"He got a layup in transition because he got out and ran. Even some of the fouls, they were just good fouls. Because he was just playing hard. Our guys felt that, responded to it, and liked it. They kind of rallied around it," Brown told reporters.

Nickel seems like a natural fit under the coach who proudly cares about the process that went into decisions more than he does their exact results. Brown's comments set the bar for the Vanderbilt product to impact games in multiple ways. The coach clearly thinks he can, whether his shot is falling or not. His coach is known to give opportunities whenever possible to ready contributors. It's simply on the player to continue to be one.

There are plenty of veterans ahead of Nickel on the team's depth chart. Brown's goal is likely to never have to rely on Nickel, or any of his two-way players, unless a member of his rotation suffers an injury. The next time the coach feels the urge to reach for the end of his bench, though, he might not have to think twice before trusting Nickel again. The rookie is 1-for-1 when it comes to rewarding his faith.

articles.title: Recap: Boston College falls to Cincinnati, 70-59
articles.summary: On Friday afternoon, the Boston College men’s basketball team faced Cincinnati in its second and final game of the ESPN Events Invitational at State Farm Fie...
articles.body:
On Friday afternoon, the Boston College men's basketball team faced Cincinnati in its second and final game of the ESPN Events Invitational at State Farm Field House in Kissimmee, FL. BC came in 7-0, a day removed from a last-second win over UCF, and as a 9.5-point underdog. The Bearcats handed BC its first loss of the season, 70-59, pulling away in the second half.

The start was promising. Tyler Tejada hit two early threes to put Cincinnati up 6-1, but BC turned five Bearcat turnovers into a 13-0 run and led 14-6 after a Money Williams layup at the 12:14 mark. Williams scored 10 points during that stretch.

Then the offense dried up. Former BC forward Jayden Hastings started a Cincinnati run with two free throws, and the Bearcats took a 20-19 lead on an Elijah Perryman layup with just over five minutes left in the half. The teams traded baskets until two Armoni Zeigler free throws gave BC a 28-27 halftime lead. Cincinnati committed 10 turnovers in the first half, and BC held an 11-3 edge in points off turnovers at the break. That's the primary reason BC was ahead.

Cincinnati cleaned that up after halftime. A Colby Duggan three put BC up 31-29, but the Bearcats scored the next six to lead 35-31. Williams tied it at 36 with a second-chance three at 15:18. Cincinnati then went on a 12-2 run, capped by a Tylen Riley steal and breakaway dunk, to lead 48-38 with 10:54 left. BC never got even again.

To BC's credit, it didn't go away. Down 52-42 with 9:02 left, BC scored five straight through Williams while Cincinnati went 3:37 without a point. Duggan's corner three later cut it to 60-57 with 3:06 left, and BC had a real chance.

Tejada ended it. He answered with a three from the right wing to make it 63-57, then hit another from the top of the key to make it 66-59 with 1:34 left. After Williams missed a three, Tejada grabbed the rebound and made both free throws to push the lead to nine. Cincinnati closed on a 10-2 spurt. Tejada finished with a game-high 24 points, 18 of them in the second half, on 7/11 shooting, 4/5 from three and 6/6 at the line.

The shooting numbers tell most of the story. BC shot 17/57 from the field, while Cincinnati shot 23/45. The Bearcats won the paint 28-12 and the bench 24-6. Cincinnati shot 56.5% after halftime, which is not something BC's defense had allowed much of through seven games. BC grabbed 17 offensive rebounds and got 14 second-chance points out of them, which kept the game close longer than it probably should have been.

Hastings, who played 62 games over two seasons at BC, had a quiet but useful game against his old team, with 7 points, 5 rebounds and 3 blocks off the bench. Perryman added 6 points, 5 assists and 4 rebounds, and was a game-best plus-18.

Williams led BC with 21 points and hit four threes. Luke Hunger added 12, Zeigler had 11, and Duggan scored 9 on three threes. Beyond Williams, nobody could create good looks consistently, and that's going to be a problem against better teams.

Losing to a good Big 12 team on a neutral floor is no disaster, but the offense needs a second option. BC falls to 7-1.

Next up, BC travels to Georgia on Tuesday for the SEC/ACC Challenge.

articles.title: Rutgers Women’s Basketball Suffers First Loss of Season, 84-68 to South Dakota State
articles.summary: Poor start dooms Rutgers against SDSU
articles.body:
After starting the season 8-0 and defeating cross-state rival Princeton, Rutgers women's basketball suffered its first loss of the season, 84-68 to South Dakota State in game one of the Daytona Beach Classic. The Scarlet Knights got off to an ugly start in this game, where they could not dig themselves out of a steep first-quarter hole that saw them down 21 points after just 10 minutes of play.

After the game was tied at 5 with just over 8 minutes to play in the first quarter, South Dakota State would go on a 12-0 run to go up 17-5 before the Knights scored again around the four-minute mark in the first quarter. Rutgers would string together four points before the Jackrabbits went on a 13-0 run to close out the quarter up 30-9.

The Knights would start to get off the mat over the next two quarters, preventing South Dakota from going on unanswered runs as they did in the first quarter, and eventually closing the gap to single digits as they headed into the fourth quarter down 63-54. However, for every shot the Knights made in the fourth quarter, the Jackrabbits had an answer. A quick three-pointer by South Dakota State's Hadley Thul at the start of the fourth would put Rutgers in another double-digit hole, one they could not recover from, as the Jackrabbits held on to secure the win.

This game highlights some early-season concerns for the Knights, who allowed the Jackrabbits to hit 49.2 percent of their total shots and 52 percent of their shots from three. On top of that, the Jackrabbits forced six more turnovers. recorded 14 more rebounds, had six more points in the paint, and had 15 more assists in their winning effort.

Brooklyn Meyer led the Jackrabbits with 20 points, with Katie Vasecka right behind her at 19. Meyer recorded a double-double on the day by scooping up 10 rebounds as well. Emilee Fox and Mali Abdouch recorded double-digit points for South Dakota State as well.

Mia Pauldo was once again the star of the show for Rutgers, recording 37 points and hitting half of her shots.

In addition to their poor defensive performance, the Knights, outside of Pauldo, failed to drum up any offensive consistency. Outside of Pauldo's 14 of 28 on all her shots, the rest of the Knights hit just nine of their 38 total shots. While Pauldo is a very effective offensive weapon, scoring has to come from other areas to supplement her efforts.

The good news is that the Knights still have time to remedy these issues before Big Ten play starts in full force. The next four games against Georgetown, St. Peter's, No.19 Ohio State and Seton Hall will provide a glimpse into what the Knights will look like for the rest of the season.

Rutgers will play Georgetown tomorrow in game two of the Daytona Beach Classic. Tip-off for the game will be at 5:45 pm.

articles.title: 3 Observations from Indiana men’s basketball’s 93-57 win over Bowling Green
articles.summary: Indiana men’s basketball cruised to a big win over Bowling Green to move to 8-0 on the season.
articles.body:
Indiana men's basketball dominated Bowling Green tonight, going on a run just over five minutes into the game that effectively put the Falcons to bed. The Hoosiers were shooting well, defending well, and rebounding well in what may have been the most complete performance from this group so far.

Though it wasn't a marquee win like last week's victories over Arkansas or Kentucky, the margin of victory was one that boosted Indiana's computer profile. KenPom only favored Indiana by 20 entering the game, so the blowout moved Indiana up five spots in the national ranking.

At 8-0, Indiana looks much improved over Darian DeVries' first season, with KenPom now projecting the Hoosiers to win 23 games and go 12-8 in Big Ten play.

Indiana had a season-high 18 assists tonight against Bowling Green, starting to resemble the fast-paced offense we saw from DeVries' group last year. While Indiana has more players that are capable of creating unassisted buckets, the ball movement tonight helped the Hoosiers take more quality looks from the perimeter, something that will be important for maintaining a respectable 3-point percentage this season.

Bryce Lindsay's deep shot against Arkansas will go down as a high-point of the season, but over the last couple games Indiana had gotten into the habit of chucking a few too many heat checks from deep or taking transition threes that negate the team's rebounding advantage.

Seeing the way the ball moved tonight was an encouraging step for this group not just cause it made the offense look a little better, but because it reflects well on the team's chemistry so early in the season. With a team full of transfers, having nine different players record an assist in a game is no small feat.

Aiden Sherrell had one of his stronger performances of the season, finishing with 16 points, nine rebounds, two blocks and an assist. He also went 2-6 from 3-point range.

Tonight's performance was a good example of why he's a potential NBA player. A seven footer who can score from the perimeter, rebound on both ends of the floor, and protect the rim is a valuable piece for any team. After an impressive year last year at Bama, he's averaging more points and shooting better from deep this year at Indiana.

Even though he cooled off by the end of the night, his early threes are exactly what Indiana will need from him going forward. Establishing himself as a threat at the beginning of the game will force defenses to account for him until the final whistle.

It's hard to say enough good things about Bryce Lindsay so far this year. Against Bowling Green, he scored 18 points, grabbed five rebounds, had three assists, and also added two steals. He was also super efficient, going 2/4 from 3-point range and making all of his free throws.

What I like most about Lindsay's game is his ability to be what DeVries needs on the floor, no matter who he's playing with. He can play point guard alongside Darren Harris at the shooting guard spot, or play shooting guard next to Markus Burton.

Calling him the sixth man doesn't even feel right, as he plays the fifth most minutes on the team, but he's been a huge asset for DeVries and Indiana this year, doing everything asked of him, and then some.

articles.title: Tennessee soccer season ends in penalty kicks vs Ohio State in NCAA 2nd round
articles.summary: Tennessee soccer almost pulled off a stunning upset against No. 1 seed Ohio State, but lost in penalty kicks to end its season in NCAA second round.
articles.body:
Tennessee soccer was on the brink of a miracle against No. 1 seed Ohio State, forcing overtime and a penalty shootout, but it didn't have enough to finish the upset.

No. 8 seed Lady Vols (8-6-4) fell to the Buckeyes (17-2-1) in a penalty shootout at Jesse Owens Memorial Stadium in Columbus, Ohio, on Nov. 27 to end their season in the NCAA Tournament second round. Ohio State won the penalty shootout 4-2, with freshman forward Ayva Jordan's shot saved by Buckeyes goalkeeper Peighton Northrup and senior forward Kylee Simmons missing off the crossbar.

The game was tied 2-2 at the end of regulation. Had the Lady Vols won, they would have faced their new coach Richard Moodie and Purdue in the third round.

The loss marks the end of the season and the beginning of a new era for Tennessee soccer, which will be led by Moodie once he finishes his tournament run with the No. 4 seed Boilermakers. He was hired Nov. 17 to replace Joe Kirt, who was fired after five seasons. Moodie led Purdue to the Sweet 16 with a 3-1 win over Houston on Nov. 27, and the Boilermakers will face Ohio State in the Sweet 16 on Nov. 30.

Tennessee went down 2-0 in the first half before rallying in the second half, tying the game off a corner kick with 7:25 left in regulation. Simmons scored the game-tying goal to send the game to overtime, and neither team could score in overtime to end it.

The Buckeyes scored almost immediately in the first half, possessing the ball through Tennessee's defense easily before sending a cross into the box, which Anika Poremba sent into the top right corner from six yards out 1:21 into the game.

Ohio State doubled the lead in the first half after Tennessee gave up a penalty kick due to a poorly-timed tackle in the box, and Ava Bramblett scored with a shot on the ground. Ohio State had 22 shots to Tennessee's nine, with 10 of them on goal.

Freshman midfielder Emerson Moore cut the deficit for the Lady Vols to 2-1 with 11:12 left in the game, scoring on a beautiful shot to the upper left corner from just outside the box.

Tennessee opened the NCAA Tournament a 3-2 win over No. 9 seed Liberty in the first round, which was its second win in the tournament in the last five seasons. The Lady Vols have made it to the second round twice since making a run to the Sweet 16 in 2021 in Brian Pensky's final season.
